chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: Why McRae switched from Conn to Selmer saxophone
summary: Welburn asks about the switch; McRae says the Conn was too weak to be heard across the packed Savoy.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I think we touched on some of that on Tuesday.
What I want to ask you about now is saxophones. You switched from a Conn to the Selmer.
Tell me when you did that, what brought it about, and what's the difference between those two horns, especially for an orchestra?
The Conn horn was a good instrumet. Conn and the King -- anything like that. It was a good instrument.

In playing the Savoy, I would notice on a Saturday night or any given big night we had up there, I could be playing that horn and like, from over (Inaudible) to the desk out there, the crowd will be so heavy that you couldn't hear me in the back, you know.
I be playing -- unless I was in the mike, something like that, then they could hear me, you know.

But then when Coleman Hawkins --
DownBeat, I think {inaudible} -- I think when Coleman
went to Europe, they had a picture of him playing
a Selmer. They were talking about the Selmer.

The Selmer came in and Selmer was trying
to get these instruments over to the dances -- break
it in America.

Selmer put in a big splash here, you
know. They would try to promote the Selmer horn.

Well -- in fact, I didn't know too much
about the Selmer. I know it was -- reading about it.
I know Coleman Hawkins was playing one in Europe.

Ol' man Selmer had gave him a horn,
a gold horn. I say, "Man, maybe I'll try one of them,"
you know.

And Benny -- I think Beeny Waters we were
talking about at the time. So I decided when we
went to the Paramount, I was going to get me a
Selmer.
